questions.stem: A pedigree shows affected individuals in every generation, both sexes affected, and an affected father with an affected son. What is the most likely inheritance?
questions.explanation: Vertical transmission with male-to-male transmission indicates AD. A, B: X-linked inheritance never shows male-to-male transmission. C: AR is horizontal (siblings). E: Mitochondrial disease isn't passed by fathers.
questions.source: Mendelian Patterns and Inheritance, reading p1

questions.stem: Two unaffected parents have a child with cystic fibrosis. What is the chance their next child will be an unaffected carrier?
questions.explanation: Each child: 25% affected, 50% carrier, 25% non-carrier. B: 25% is the risk of being affected. C: 75% is the chance of being unaffected. D: 2/3 is the carrier probability for an already unaffected sibling. E: Not all children are carriers.
questions.source: Mendelian Patterns and Inheritance, reading p3

questions.stem: A man with Marfan syndrome has an unaffected daughter whose son has Marfan syndrome. What explains the daughter's status?
questions.explanation: She carries the mutation but shows no phenotype: non-penetrance. A: Variable expressivity is differing severity in affected carriers. B: Mosaicism would involve her father's gonads. C: Anticipation is worsening over generations from repeat expansion. D: Pleiotropy is multiple effects of one gene.
questions.source: Mendelian Patterns and Inheritance, reading p2

questions.stem: A man with hemophilia A and a non-carrier woman have children. What is the risk to their sons and daughters?

options.B: 50% of sons affected; 50% of daughters carriers
options.C: No sons affected; all daughters carriers

questions.explanation: An affected male gives his X to all daughters (carriers) and his Y to all sons. A: Sons get his Y. B: That's the pattern for a carrier mother. D: Sons aren't carriers. E: Daughters are heterozygous carriers, usually unaffected.
questions.source: Mendelian Patterns and Inheritance, reading p3

questions.stem: A girl has progressive proximal weakness and markedly elevated CK. Dystrophin testing shows a pathogenic variant on one X; her father is healthy. Which mechanism best explains her symptoms?
questions.explanation: If most cells inactivate the normal X, a heterozygous female can manifest an X-linked recessive disease. A: UPD is possible but far less common than skewing. C: DMD isn't a repeat disease. D: Pseudodominance relates to consanguinity in AR. E: Dystrophin isn't imprinted.
questions.source: Mendelian Patterns and Inheritance, reading p4

questions.stem: Unaffected parents have two children with achondroplasia, both carrying the same FGFR3 mutation. Neither parent has the mutation in blood DNA. What best explains the recurrence?
questions.explanation: A mutation in part of a parent's germline can recur in several gametes. A: Achondroplasia is fully penetrant, so a carrier parent would be affected. B: It's dominant. C: Not a repeat disorder. D: The same gene is involved.
questions.source: Mendelian Patterns and Inheritance, reading p2

questions.stem: Hereditary deafness can be caused by mutations in many different genes with AD, AR, or X-linked inheritance. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Different genes causing the same phenotype is locus heterogeneity. A: Allelic heterogeneity is different mutations in one gene. B: Pleiotropy is one gene with multiple effects. D: Variable expressivity is varying severity. E: A phenocopy is a non-genetic mimic (e.g., rubella deafness).
questions.source: Mendelian Patterns and Inheritance, reading p5

questions.stem: A healthy woman's brother and maternal uncle both have hemophilia A. Her parents are unaffected. What is the probability that her first son will be affected?
questions.explanation: Her mother is an obligate carrier (affected son and affected brother), so the woman has a 1/2 chance of being a carrier, and a carrier's son has a 1/2 risk: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. A: That's the risk if she were a known carrier. C: 1/8 is the risk for a child of unknown sex. D: 2/3 is the carrier risk of an unaffected sibling in AR disease. E: Unaffected women can still be carriers.
questions.source: Mendelian Patterns and Inheritance, slides 45–46; reading p3–4

questions.stem: Different FGFR3 mutations cause achondroplasia, hypochondroplasia, thanatophoric dysplasia, or craniosynostosis. What does the lecture call this?
questions.explanation: One gene producing several distinct phenotypes is clinical heterogeneity. B: Locus heterogeneity is many genes causing one phenotype (e.g., deafness). C: Penetrance is whether a carrier shows any phenotype. D: Germline mosaicism explains recurrence from unaffected parents. E: A phenocopy is a non-genetic mimic.
